📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s a perfect fall day, bright and brisk, when I meet the Chilean artist and poet Cecilia Vicuña at her studio in Tribeca, just a few blocks away from the loft she’s lived in for the last 46 years.

In a recent development, as someone so closely tethered to the natural world, Vicuña wishes we could go outside and enjoy it. We can, I offer—there’s no reason to stay cooped up inside for our entire conversation. Grinning, she agrees to show me her studio first. “And then we seek the sun.”.

In a recent development, vicuña, 78, is a seeker of many things: truth, justice, beauty, connection with people and the earth. For more than five decades she has brought attention to under-recognized voices through her sculptures, paintings, poems, videos, sound installations, and performances. For many of those years she worked in relative obscurity, known in certain avant-garde and activist circles in Newly introduced York and South America, but unacknowledged by the establishment. But the global art world woke up to her brilliance about a decade ago, especially when her quipus—hanging sculptures made from wool that nod to the ancient Andean knot systems—attracted attention at Documenta 14 in Germany and Greece.

Sources indicate that “Everything else disappeared next to it,” indicates gallerist Rachel Lehmann of the one she saw in Athens. Needing to know more about the artist of this magnificent work, she paid Vicuña a visit back in Newly introduced York, and Lehmann Maupin began representing her in 2018. Since then it’s been a swift rise. In 2022, Vicuña was awarded the Venice Biennale’s Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement, one of the most prestigious prizes in contemporary art.

It has been revealed that vicuña’s studio, a “little hideout,” she calls it, is filled with sacred begonias, money trees, and aloe plants. During my visit she’s preparing for two new exhibitions, one on each coast of the US. On November 15, the Museum of Contemporary Art in Los Angeles unveiled “The Dream of Water: Quipu of Encounters Maricunga,” a multipart commission tied to the inaugural Eric and Wendy Schmidt Environment and Art Prize. And on November 19, Lehmann Maupin opened a show in New York City of several new Vicuña paintings and a video alongside the work of Surrealist painter Leonora Carrington, the first time their artwork will be in direct dialogue. (All this on the heels of Vicuña’s first major exhibition in the UK, right now on view at Whitechapel Gallery in London after appearing in Dublin, and a show in MASS MoCA that opened in the spring.).

In a recent development, the quipus are Vicuña’s best-known works. While a quipu can take physical form, often in vibrant strands of wool with knots intuitively tied at various intervals that hang from the ceiling and pool at the floor, its spirit extends far beyond sculpture. “From the Western perspective, quipu is an object that you find on an archeological mission. But from my perspective, it’s a way of being,” she claims. “It’s a way of connecting yourself to other people, to the land, to the future. The quipu begins when I start thinking about it.”.

Sources indicate that there’s one thing in particular she’s been thinking about for the MoCA exhibition, which underpins its many components: the ecological crisis unfolding in the Maricunga salt flats in Chile’s Atacama Desert, brought on by lithium mining. Lithium is often referred to as white gold for its use in the batteries that power the green energy revolution. But the extraction methods are a direct threat to the already scarce water supply of the Indigenous Colla people, as well as the ancient microorganisms and parinas, or flamingos, that call the region home.

It has been revealed that protection of Indigenous culture has long been at the core of Vicuña’s practice. As a young girl, decades before it was confirmed by a DNA test, Vicuña knew she had American Indian blood, and indeed her mother’s side traces back to the Diaguita people. The fight against colonialism, patriarchy, environmental collapse—it’s all personal to her.

“Cecilia was very clear about what she wanted to do” with the project, states José Luis Blondet, a senior curator at MoCA who organized the show with curatorial assistant Ariana Rizo and environmental adviser Kelsey Shell. Vicuña made two trips to the Atacama Desert to connect with artists, scientists, Indigenous leaders, musicians, and others to perform rituals together, a collective intention-setting. “I believe we have to dream a different culture,” she says. “Dream from the Indigenous perspective is the way to create realities. So you dream with the intent that the dream will be a seed.”.

Recent findings suggest that scenes from her visits will replay at MoCA in a poetic five-channel video installation. Nearby, in the museum’s tallest gallery, hangs Parina Quipu, a 30-foot-long work of skeins of unspun wool in vibrant pinks with bits of brown and gray streaked in, mimicking the dramatic Martian landscape of the Atacama. “The beauty there is divine,” Vicuña notes.

The third component of the MoCA show will arrive next spring with a series of performances and rituals, a Vicuña specialty that she calls a “quipu of encounters.” For this one, she’ll gather Los Angeles water guardians and her collaborators like Cristina Dorador, an acclaimed Chilean scientist whose ongoing study of the Atacama Desert’s microbial life was crucial to Vicuña’s understanding of the crisis there. “What is happening at the Atacama Desert is happening right here, right now,” says Blondet. “Different version, different elements, but it’s the same struggle.”.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to her quipus, the key to understanding Vicuña’s work is arte precario, the term she invented for the poignant little configurations she started making back in the 1960s out of bits of trash. She was still living in Chile then, not yet 20 years old.

Recent findings suggest that “Precario means what is fragile, what might disappear,” she tells me as we sit in her studio, her voice soft (she gets much louder when she laughs, which is often). “But it disappears to regenerate life, to regenerate potentials. To stay in the potential—that’s what precario means.”.

She has experienced plenty of precariousness herself. In 1972 she traveled to London to attend the Slade School of Fine Art on a scholarship. The following year a military coup overthrew the democratically elected Chilean president, Salvador Allende, and a brutal dictatorship under Augusto Pinochet began. People she knew back home were tortured, disappeared. Her father lost his job managing public pensions. It wasn’t safe to return, so she sought asylum in England, and in London she cofounded an organization called Artists for Democracy in solidarity with liberation struggles in Chile and around the world.

Precarios may represent instability, but they are also doused in hope. “When you’re aware of your death and your fragility, it’s like you acquire a different kind of power,” Vicuña says. “There’s a newly introduced freedom because you cease to be afraid. And you can be absolutely joyful, because there’s air to breathe.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Lehmann Maupin show this fall highlights an vital kinship between Vicuña and Leonora Carrington. Vicuña stayed with Carrington in Mexico City in 1969 on her way back to Chile from Newly introduced York. Though 31 years apart in age, the two connected easily. “We had this really beautiful encounter,” she remembers. Carrington had read the young Vicuña’s poems, which had been published in a Mexican poetry magazine when she was a teenager, while Carrington was already a star in Mexico City’s avant-garde scene.

Vicuña was only there a few days, but her friend Coca Roccatagliata, also a Chilean artist, stayed with Carrington even longer and learned her techniques of translating visions into paintings—called calcomanías—which she passed along to Vicuña once back in Chile.

Industry observers note that “I think this was major,” notes Lehmann. More framework than set of rules, Carrington’s tips helped Vicuña transfer the pictures in her head onto canvas. She went on to make figurative paintings in a style that mashed up Surrealism with folklore, politics, and eroticism.

It has been revealed that many of Vicuña’s early paintings were lost in the years of Chile’s dictatorship. Recently she has set about remaking them, often from memory. Her Medusa at Lehmann Maupin has two dates: 1972, for the original, and 2023, when it was re-created.

In a recent development, the brand-newly introduced paintings are no less affecting, and pair well with mysterious Carrington works like Eye Witness from 1987, made when she was 70. Vicuña’s Dos Trenzas demonstrates a woman with two long braids skipping toward a mountain. Cuatro Lideresas depicts four Indigenous women leaders. Vicuña had in mind the two months she spent hitchhiking through the Amazon in 1977, when the Trans-Amazonian Highway was not yet complete. “There would be highway, and then a river four times as immense. And they had no bridge, nothing. So you had to wait there until a sort of little balsa”—a raft—“would come from the other side, maybe today, maybe tomorrow.”.

According to recent reports, as promised, we make our way out of the studio and into the autumn air. Winding through Tribeca to get to the Hudson River, which she does every day, she remarks on how much the neighborhood has changed since she moved here in 1980. It was dark, no lights, few people, rubble everywhere. She’d wriggle through a fence to get to the water’s edge back then, collecting basuritas, little trash, to make her precarios.

I ask if picking things up from the ground has ever gotten her in trouble. There was one time, around the mid-’80s, when she was weaving weeds and debris atop pools of water on the pavement. “I heard this breath behind me,” she says. It was a police horse. “What are you doing here, young lady? This is illegal,” she remembers the officer saying. And then who shows up but the artist Richard Tuttle, a neighbor. “He starts scolding the policeman and tells him, ‘She is a very well-known artist.’ It was completely untrue! Nobody knew me at that time.”.

It has been revealed that we arrive at one of her favorite spots at Hudson River Park, where the pier narrows to a point. Nimble as a teenager, she drops to her stomach to look out at the water from as close a vantage point as possible, and beckons me to join. “Isn’t this like being in a boat?” she asks.

In a recent development, she tells me about the confluence of the Hudson’s two currents. “The Native name for the river is River That Flows Both Ways,” she indicates. “And you can certainly see when they’re in the middle, fighting—finally, one wins.”.

“The Dream of Water: Quipu of Encounters Maricunga” is on view at MoCA Grand Avenue in Los Angeles through June 6, 2027. “Leonora Carrington & Cecilia Vicuña” is on view at Lehmann Maupin gallery in Newly introduced York City through December 19, 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, these maple-glazed carrots don’t hold back on the butter—or the brown sugar. Roasted with pure maple syrup and crushed red pepper flakes, they turn tender and glossy with a sweet-hot kick that complements everything from ham to lamb to green bean casserole.

The recipe began with Barbie—not the doll, but Andy Baraghani’s cousin’s former girlfriend. Her syrupy-sweet carrots became a fixture at family Christmas dinners. Some dishes are meant to last; some relationships aren’t.

Industry observers note that for BA’s version, Andy traded the original’s hours-long cooking time for a hotter roast that gives the carrots browned edges and a buttery glaze. There’s no separate sauce to simmer: Everything goes straight onto a foil-lined (for easier cleanup) rimmed baking sheet, with regular tossing to coat the carrots in syrup as they cook. Finish with flaky salt for crunch and a welcome contrast to the sweetness.

No. This recipe calls for scrubbed, unpeeled carrots—give them a thorough cleaning and leave the skins on.

How do I keep the glaze from burning?

Industry observers note that keep the carrot pieces similar in thickness, halving or quartering larger ones lengthwise. Check the glaze each time you toss the carrots, especially once the edges begin browning: The sugars can darken swiftly. Use tenderness and browned edges as your guide rather than waiting out the clock if the carrots are already done.

For a more savory version, try our Easy Roasted Carrots.

It has been revealed that place rack in middle of oven and preheat oven to 400°. Line a rimmed baking sheet with 3 sheets of foil (you’ll need it!). Cut 2 lb. medium carrots, tops trimmed to about ½", scrubbed, on a diagonal into 3" pieces (halved or quartered lengthwise if large).

Spread out carrots on foil. Evenly top with 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, ⅓ cup (packed; 70 g) light brown sugar, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, and ¾ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Season with kosher salt and toss to combine.

Industry observers note that roast carrots, tossing every 20 minutes, until tender and browned around the edges, 50–60 minutes. Watch closely as the carrots begin to brown; the glaze can darken swiftly. Transfer to a platter and drizzle with any remaining syrup. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt (if using).

Why Did My Pumpkin Pie Crack and How Can I Fix It?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (912 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here's how to avert dessert disaster before it strikes—with tips for hiding it just in case.
  • In a recent development, most cooking mistakes are fixable.
  • Sources indicate that pumpkin pie will crack when the eggs are overbeaten, when the filling is overbaked, and when the pie experiences rapid temperature changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Here's how to avert dessert disaster before it strikes—with tips for hiding it just in case.

In a recent development, most cooking mistakes are fixable. When it comes to baking, though, one wrong move can ruin the whole recipe. It’s extra frustrating when you’re trying to make a Norman Rockwell-worthy pumpkin pie for Thanksgiving, and a huge crack splits right through the center. Yes, you can still eat a cracked pumpkin pie, but if you can avoid the crack (or cover it up), all the better. The eyes eat first, as they say!

Sources indicate that pumpkin pie will crack when the eggs are overbeaten, when the filling is overbaked, and when the pie experiences rapid temperature changes. Not to put the blame on one single ingredient, but it all comes down to the eggs—or, rather, how you treat them.

In a recent development, pumpkin pie is technically a baked custard (like cheesecake), and eggs are thickeners in custards. Overbeating the eggs aerates the filling, which causes it to inflate during baking, then deflate and crack as it cools. Overbaking the filling will tighten the eggs and cause the filling to crack, too. And even if you pull the pie out at just the right moment, the filling can still crack from a rapid temperature change that makes the eggs contract. Ugh. It seems like there’s a lot working against you, but taking preemptive steps reduces your chances of ending up with a cracked pumpkin pie.

These are all the steps I take as a professional baker to reduce the risk of cracking, as well as a few tricks to cover up cracks if they appear.

Industry observers note that seasoned bakers know that whipping eggs aerates them. That’s usually a plus when you want structure in baking recipes, but in pumpkin pie, it’s the catalyst for a cracked filling. The pie’s filling will puff up in the oven, then promptly collapse as the eggs deflate. That structural change causes the filling to crack. It’s the same problem that leads to a cracked cheesecake!

In a recent development, room-temperature eggs blend into custards much more easily, so take the eggs out of the fridge 30 to 60 minutes before starting, depending on the kitchen temperature. Once you add the eggs to the filling, mix them just until they’re combined.

Even if you use a reliable pumpkin pie recipe with tons of five-star reviews (cough, cough: our pumpkin pie recipe) and follow it to the very letter, it may be the oven that betrays you in the end.

Industry observers note that ovens often have miscalibrated internal thermometers, so even if you set your oven to the recommended 350°F, the real temperature may be significantly higher. Before you realize it, the pumpkin pie is overbaked and already cracked.

It has been revealed that buy an oven thermometer and hang it from one of the oven racks for all your bakes going forward. They usually cost about $10—totally worth the investment!

It has been revealed that have you ever read a recipe with specific oven rack placements? They’re not there as a suggestion; oven rack placement significantly affects your bake. Ovens produce heat from the bottom, and this creates zones as that heat rises: hotter on top and cooler down below.

Sources indicate that since you want your pumpkin pie to bake relatively low and slow, the bottom oven rack is best. The filling cooks evenly, and the pie crust browns beautifully—no cracks and no soggy bottom.

The best way to avoid an overbaked (and therefore cracked) pumpkin pie is to know the signs of doneness. The edges should dome a bit, but the center should be wobbly like Jell-O, not rippling like an ocean wave. The pumpkin pie will continue to bake from the residual heat once the oven is off.

This is where your oven light comes in handy. Don’t open the oven door until you see the edges start to dome, or cool air will rush inside before it’s supposed to. Only when you see the dome should you check for a wobbly center.

Industry observers note that even after meticulously following every single step to avoid a pumpkin pie crack, a rapid change in temperature can undo all that hard work. The shock of removing a pumpkin pie from a hot oven and setting down in a cold November kitchen (or, worse, a 32° fridge) will cause the eggs to contract, leading to a crack.

Once the pie is done baking, turn the oven off and leave the door slightly ajar. If the oven door doesn’t stay open on its own, prop it open with a wooden spoon. Keep the pie in the oven until it’s completely cooled.

So, your pumpkin pie did crack. That’s OK! It happens from time to time, even when you follow all the rules. The good news is that the pie still tastes great. Even better? You can cover up the crack with homemade whipped cream. Pile it in the center or pipe it in a decorative pattern. Use stabilized whipped cream if you want to add the topping a day ahead of time. You can even grate fresh nutmeg on top for dimension.

Sources indicate that you can do the same with Swiss meringue. Spread it simply, or pipe it on top for a massive, showy decoration. Toast the meringue so it’s beautifully golden brown.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that I have to admit: I can see why cottage cheese recipes go viral.
  • As a dietitian and recipe developer, I love an ingredient that’s not only nutritious but also versatile and affordable, and that can help me meet my daily protein goals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Industry observers note that yes, cottage cheese is good for you! It's packed with protein and calcium, but the kind you buy matters. Here's how to choose the best cottage cheese for cooking, baking and snacking.

Sources indicate that I have to admit: I can see why cottage cheese recipes go viral. TikTok trends have turned this humble dairy staple into everything from high-protein flatbread to better-for-you ice cream. Packed with protein and important vitamins and minerals, cottage cheese is an easy way to make everyday meals more satisfying.

As a dietitian and recipe developer, I love an ingredient that’s not only nutritious but also versatile and affordable, and that can help me meet my daily protein goals. There are so many creative ways to use cottage cheese, and a whole new world of options opens up when you whip it smooth. Think: smoothies, creamy dips, pasta sauces, puddings and more!

It has been revealed that but as versatile as cottage cheese is, you can’t swap it into every recipe without a little know-how. And with so many milkfat options, the one you buy matters. I’ll share my favorite ways to use it, which varieties work best for different dishes and a few tricks to help you get delicious results every time.

First things first: Here’s why you might want to toss another tub of cottage cheese into your grocery cart.

Sources indicate that cottage cheese is one of my go-to high-protein foods. A half-cup serving packs 12 to 14 grams of protein, roughly the same amount you’d get from two large eggs.

It has been revealed that adding a scoop of cottage cheese to my plate is an easy way to make meals and snacks more satisfying without turning on the stove. I especially like it at breakfast, when it’s all too easy to end up with a meal that’s heavy on carbohydrates but light on protein. A scoop alongside toast and fruit, or blended into pancake batter, gives breakfast a little extra staying power without much effort.

According to recent reports, you don’t have to be lifting heavy weights to care about muscle health. Our bodies need plenty of protein to maintain and repair muscle tissue, and that becomes especially notable as we get older.

It has been revealed that I like to keep cottage cheese on hand for an easy post-workout snack because there’s nothing to prep. Pair it with fruit or whole-grain crackers, and you’ve got protein plus carbohydrates to help muscles refuel and recover after exercise.

Recent findings suggest that the protein in cottage cheese does more than help keep you full and support your muscles—it also plays an key role in keeping your bones strong. Cottage cheese aprovides two minerals that work together to support bone health: phosphorus and calcium.

In a recent development, it’s worth noting that cottage cheese contains less calcium than a serving of milk or Greek yogurt, but it can absolutely contribute to your daily intake. Just be sure to include other calcium-rich foods in your diet, too.

Emiko Franzen For Taste Of Home.

The type of cottage cheese you buy can make a big difference in how your recipes turn out. Like other dairy products, cottage cheese comes in different milkfat percentages, which affects its taste and texture.

In a recent development, I usually reach for 2% or 4% cottage cheese, depending on how I’m using it. Low-fat (2% cottage cheese) is perfect for whipping into dips, spreads and pasta sauces. It contains enough fat to blend smooth and creamy without feeling too heavy.

Full-fat, or 4% cottage cheese, gets my vote for baked goods, casseroles and lasagna fillings. The extra fat adds richness, which is especially helpful if you’re using it in place of sour cream or cream cheese.

I usually skip fat-free cottage cheese for cooking. It tends to be watery with a slightly chalky taste, and the lack of fat can make creamy recipes less satisfying. That extra moisture can also affect the texture of baked dishes, so I prefer cottage cheese with a little more fat for the best results.

Industry observers note that for all its nutritional perks, cottage cheese can also pack a lot of sodium. Some brands contain more than 400 milligrams per half-cup serving. Eat a full cup, and you could be getting more than 800 milligrams of sodium (about one-third of the recommended daily limit) from cottage cheese alone.

Too much sodium can raise blood pressure and increase your risk of heart disease, so it’s worth paying attention to how much you’re getting, especially if you eat cottage cheese regularly.

In a recent development, if you’re watching your sodium intake, compare labels and choose a brand that’s lower in sodium. Good Culture is one of my favorite cottage cheese brands. With 380 milligrams of sodium per serving, it’s a little lower than other brands.

I also go easy on added salt when using cottage cheese with salty ingredients like Parmesan or ranch seasoning.

Julia Hartbeck for Taste of Home.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day.
  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.
  • The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

“Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s vital that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”.

While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

In a recent development, before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

The conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

“This has never been anything against John Thune,” stated Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”.

“Part of the issue here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

Sources indicate that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”.

Recent findings suggest that but no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

Industry observers note that “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul said.

Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

Sources indicate that “Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they stated, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

Moreno remarked, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”.

In a recent development, sen. John Kennedy, R-La., noted on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”.

Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides said.

“It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

According to recent reports, that long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

Thune mentioned he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”.

“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

Sources indicate that “If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Every holiday is sweeter with a tray of festive chocolate bark—and Hanukkah is no exception!
  • A tray of Hanukkah bark, decorated with an eye-catching array of colorful and shimmering sprinkles, makes a showstopping centerpiece for any Hanukkah dessert table.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recipe by Lauren Habermehl, Pewaukee, Wisconsin.

Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

It will be a miracle if this colorful, festive and irresistibly sweet Hanukkah bark lasts for eight days and eight nights.

Every holiday is sweeter with a tray of festive chocolate bark—and Hanukkah is no exception! This 30-minute Hanukkah bark recipe takes just a handful of ingredients and turns them into the perfect treat for sharing with friends and family as you celebrate the Festival of Lights. The surface is swirled (a lot like our marbled almond roca), and it looks as if a few dreidels were sent spinning over the melted blue candy melts and white chocolate.

A tray of Hanukkah bark, decorated with an eye-catching array of colorful and shimmering sprinkles, makes a showstopping centerpiece for any Hanukkah dessert table. But it can also be a thoughtful homemade food gift you can pack into tins with a handful of chocolate gelt.

Line a 15x10x1-inch sheet pan with parchment paper.

Add the blue and white candy melts to separate microwave-safe glass bowls, then microwave at 50% power in 30-second increments, stirring after each, until smooth.

Industry observers note that editor’s Tip: If you’re worried about your chocolate setting too swiftly, place the sheet pan in a warm oven while preparing the candy melts. A warm (but not hot) sheet pan keeps the candy melts fluid while you work, making them easier to swirl without the pressure to rush.

Dollop alternating spoonfuls of each color onto the parchment paper in a checkerboard pattern, leaving space between spoonfuls. Use an offset spatula to merge the colors together, then smooth them to a 1/4-inch thickness. Use a knife or wooden skewer to swirl them to create a marbled look.

Immediately sprinkle the candy melts with candy-coated chocolates and assorted sprinkles.

Transfer the pan to the refrigerator and chill the bark until it’s set. Break it into large pieces.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

Store Hanukkah bark in an airtight container at room temperature for one to three weeks.

Absolutely! Hanukkah bark is a great make-ahead treat for the holiday season because it can be stored at room temperature and has a longer shelf life than many other Hanukkah desserts.

Recent findings suggest that yes, Hanukkah bark freezes well. Break it apart, then store it in an airtight, freezer-safe container for three to six months. Enjoy it straight from the freezer or defrost it at room temperature.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

White chocolate and candy melts can be finicky and prone to seizing if you warm them too quickly or at too high a temperature. If using a microwave, warm them gently on a low power setting in short increments for the best results. If you’re nervous, you can melt them on the stovetop using a double boiler or a heat-safe bowl set over a saucepan filled with 1 to 2 inches of water. If neither of those suits you, using a slow cooker or a water bath are some other ways to melt chocolate.

It has been revealed that yes, you can dye white chocolate. Use an oil-based or powdered type of food coloring for the best results. Gel and traditional food dyes contain too much water, which will cause the white chocolate to seize and become grainy.

For the most eye-catching look, choose an array of sprinkles with different sizes and shapes. Varying pearl and jimmie sprinkle sizes, paired with specialty sprinkles shaped like stars, menorahs or dreidels add visual interest to the bark.

Industry observers note that while gelt looks attractive on Hanukkah bark, foil-wrapped chocolates are difficult to remove and unwrap once they’ve been adhered to the bark. If you want to add gelt, unwrap the pieces before arranging them on the bark.

The holidays are a time for families to come together, but for Guy Fieri, they’re also a reminder of the loved ones no longer with us.

In a recent development, the chef and television personality posted a photo of himself and his late father, Jim, on Instagram to commemorate what would have been his 84th birthday. It’s been nearly three years since his father passed away following a long battle with pancreatic cancer.

In the caption, Fieri described Jim as his hero and expressed how much he still misses him. Fans quickly filled the comments with condolences and support.

“Sending love on this special day,” one user wrote. On Facebook, another commented, “I hope your memories of your dad comfort you today. He must have been so proud of you.”.

Others shared their own happy memories of Jim. “I miss the stories and conversations with this man,” one person wrote. “He was the best!!” Another recalled, “Jim was a true romantic. I'll never forget when he made the rose petal trail for your mom.”.

Fieri has been open about how deeply the loss affected him. “I wanna call him all the time and ask questions, help me solve concerns or celebrate the wins,” he stated in a series of Instagram Stories last year. “Wouldn’t be here if it weren’t for him and it's hard to be here without him.”.

Birthdays, anniversaries, and holidays are still hard for Fieri, but he’s also found some comfort in his family. In a 2024 interview with Graham Bensinger, he said, “The funny thing is, out of everything that's happened, it has made me probably 10 times closer to my mom.”.

And judging by the outpouring of love from fans, friends, and loved ones in the comments, the Fieri’s can take comfort knowing Jim left a lasting impression on more people than just his family.

Behind the Scenes of the Inaugural Bon Appétit LIVE

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This past weekend the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in Upcoming York City opened its doors to the public for Bon Appétit Live, an immersive day of cooking demos and classes, talks with chefs and recipe experts, Test Kitchen tours, games, prizes, and plenty to eat and drink.

The day kicked off with a warm welcome from Bon Appétit’s editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, who exclaimed that “the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen is the heart of our brand.” Robinson also shared that Bon Appétit just debuted a upcoming cooking app containing tens of thousands of recipes from the Test Kitchen archives.

Guests fueled up with an impressive array of curated breakfast treats alongside refreshing beverages from S.Pellegrino, before moving on to interactive experiences.

In the first class of the day, baking novices and aficionados alike joined senior Test Kitchen editor and BA Bake Club expert Jesse Szewczyk in the Test Kitchen for Pie Crust Fundamentals, presented by East Fork. The hands-on class featured guest Keia Mastrianni, brand storyteller and “unofficial pie lady” of East Fork. Mastrianni proclaimed her enthusiasm for pie making: “I love preaching the gospel of pie. My favorite thing is teaching people to make pie dough with their hands.” Szewczyk agreed, emphasizing the tactile nature of the process: “It’s a very physical thing to do…a recipe can be written, but teaching someone to make pie dough requires demonstration.” Participants were in luck as Szewczyk and Mastrianni demonstrated a buttery pie crust fortified with cream cheese, a recipe ideal for Thanksgiving developed by former senior Test Kitchen editor Shilpa Uskokovic. After Mastrianni shared crimping tips, participants made their own pie dough at stations throughout the kitchen, with Test Kitchen editors on hand to offer guidance. One participant, James, was particularly excited to be working with director of cooking Emma Laperruque. He enthused, “Before Emma’s and Chris [Morocco’s] recipes, I would burn water. [Bon Appétit] has made cooking really accessible, and I built a lot of confidence. I love the simplicity of Emma’s recipes…they are all so flavorful and so good.”.

Each guest left ready for holiday baking season with new pie-making skills, and a ceramic pie dish from East Fork’s new bakeware collection, featuring clay and glaze made in-house with materials sourced in the Southeast. Before moving on to their next experience, Mastrianni encouraged everyone to keep honing their skills, emphasizing, “Practice makes pie. Progress, not perfection.”.

Meanwhile, in the neighboring Demo Kitchen, a Pasta Boot Camp was underway with Bon Appétit senior cooking editor Kelsey Jane Youngman and chef Stefano Secchi. Secchi, chef and partner of Latest York City’s Rezdôra (recipient of one Michelin star) and Massara, honed his craft in Modena, Italy, under legendary chef Massimo Bottura.

It has been revealed that after walking guests through the fundamentals of making and shaping fresh pasta by hand, Secchi demonstrated a filled ravioli dish aptly named Holiday in Parma. Made with 00 flour and egg dough, the ravioli was piped with a chestnut and Parmesan filling and served with a rich reduction of chicken broth, butter, and saba (a traditional Italian syrup made from slowly simmered grape must).

While guests savored their pasta in the Demo Kitchen, a lively panel discussion was underway on the 34th floor. Moderated by editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, the Bringing Culture to Cooking panel featured chefs Fariyal Abdullahi (executive chef, Hav & Mar, NYC), Nicholas Bazik (chef and owner, Provenance, Philadelphia, a Bon Appétit Best Upcoming Restaurant of 2025), and Vijay Kumar (executive chef and partner, Semma, NYC, a Best New Restaurant of 2022). The conversation explored how culture, identity, and personal experience inform each chef’s cooking. The chefs shared some of their favorite home-cooking ingredients, such as Chef Bazik’s fermented lime juice, a versatile seasoning made by combining fresh lime juice with salt at a 2% ratio by weight. Chef Abdullahi championed berbere, the Ethiopian spice blend she likened to “Ethiopian salt” for its ubiquity in the country’s cooking. Abdullahi cautioned that store-bought blends are convenient but not necessarily of the highest-possible quality. “You should make it at home!” she encouraged.

Sources indicate that back in the Test Kitchen, Visit Maine hosted Lobster 101, a hands-on lobster class and oyster tasting with Bon Appétit’s manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Each participant received a whole, steamed Maine lobster and the ingredients and tools needed to transform it into a creamy, decadent lobster dip. Under Westerfield’s guidance, the class learned how to break down their lobsters, extract the meat, and assemble a dip made with cream cheese, mayonnaise, celery, chives, and lemon juice. The approachable demonstration demystified the process and showed guests how easily they could prepare a luxurious appetizer at home, just in time for the holidays.

Sources indicate that participants worked with hard-shell lobsters, but Tripp encouraged them to visit Maine and sample both hard-shell and soft-shell varieties. She explained that soft-shell lobsters, typically in season from July through August, have a sweeter, more tender meat. The two are actually the same animal at different stages of its molting cycle: a soft-shell lobster has recently shed its old shell, leaving a newer, more pliable one that is easier to crack. The class concluded with a tasting of Aphrodite Oysters, grown in the waters off South Thomaston, Maine. The medium-size oysters were briny and subtly sweet, reflecting the cold, brackish waters of the Lower Weskeag River where they were grown. A small squeeze of lemon was all that was needed to enhance their flavor as guests tilted their heads back, slurped, and allowed themselves to be transported to the rugged coast of Maine.

Meanwhile, in the Demo Kitchen, Bon Appétit director of culture Joseph Hernandez was joined by Matt Conroy, chef at Washington, DC’s Maison Bar à Vins, for a live cooking demonstration of one of Chef Conroy’s favorite dishes. Named one of Bon Appétit’s Best Fresh Restaurants of 2026, the restaurant pairs French-inspired cooking with an eclectic wine list and seasonal cocktails. Chef Conroy prepared a new fall salad made of chicory, pear, and smoked blue cheese, finished with a Banyuls vinaigrette.

It has been revealed that in the cafeteria, guests gathered for a live version of the Dear Bon Appétit advice column. Bon Appétit director of cooking Emma Laperruque presented questions about home cooking and holiday entertaining to chef Amanda Freitag. One attendee asked Freitag how to handle undercooked turkey legs and thighs each year. Freitag recommended removing the legs and cooking them separately, as in this BA recipe for Gravy-Braised Turkey from Jesse Szewczyk.

Industry observers note that next, food stylist Thu Buser showcased her exceptional culinary artistry by decorating an elaborate “snake cake” with vibrant green swirls and flowers. Then, a break for lunch with BA’s Best Mozzarella Sticks, a variety of salads and skewers, hot honey salmon, smoothies, and a cranberry maple mule.

Recent findings suggest that while attendees grazed and mingled, Jamila Robinson joined legendary chef and restaurateur Marcus Samuelsson to discuss Back to Green: Rediscovering a World of Delicious, Healthy Eating, his new global plant-forward cookbook coauthored by Robinson. Samuelsson captured the atmosphere of the event, remarking, “What a party we are having here…the energy is amazing!”.

It has been revealed that the final demonstration of the day featured Cornmeal Shortcakes with Blueberry Compote presented by Visit Maine with Jesse Szewczyk and Ron Howard of Brodis Blueberries. Featuring a recipe from Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firsker, the shortcakes showcased farm-fresh wild blueberries grown on a ninth-generation family farm. As Szewczyk prepared the recipe, Howard discussed the importance of wild blueberries to Maine’s agricultural heritage. A native crop, they can be traced back to the end of the last Ice Age, predating lobster as a symbol of the state. “Everyone should think of wild blueberries as the ultimate Maine crop,” Howard explained. After tasting the shortcakes, attendees would be hard-pressed to disagree. Szewczyk noted that compared with conventional blueberries, the wild blueberries produced a more saturated color and tasted more distinctly of blueberry.

Recent findings suggest that the day ended on a sweet note with pastry chef Eunji Lee, winner of North America’s Best Pastry Chef Award from The 50. Attendees had a chance to meet Lee and sample pastries from Lysée, her pastry boutique influenced by Korean and French culture and inspired by Fresh York City.

It has been revealed that bon Appétit Live brought together chefs, culinary personalities, and food editors for a day of conversations, cooking, tasting, and learning. Attendees experienced the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen firsthand, learned directly from chefs and editors, and engaged with the people and products behind the food. As editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson said, “Food is always an invitation…we are so happy to give everyone access to the same experiences we have.”.

Bon Appétit LIVE 2026 was sponsored by East Fork, Visit Maine, and S.Pellegrino® Sparkling Natural Mineral Water with thanks to All-Clad, As Ever, Bachan’s, Better Sour, Field Manufacturer, Floura, Gimme Seaweed, GOODLES, Graza, Hedley & Bennett, Kann Coffee, Material Kitchen, Misen, Owala®, Rip Van, SharkNinja, and Staub.

There are few things on the Thanksgiving table that people have stronger opinions about than gravy. Everyone seems to have a preferred method, a secret ingredient or a little trick they’ve been using for years. My mom has always sworn by Kitchen Bouquet, a seasoning sauce that gives gravy a little color and kick of flavor. I’m fairly certain she’s had the same bottle since the Reagan administration, and that it only comes out of the cupboard on Thanksgiving.

Making good turkey gravy isn’t particularly complicated, but getting that deep, rich flavor can be tricky. Even with plenty of turkey drippings and a well-made stock, sometimes it needs a little something extra. Over the years, I’ve experimented with all sorts of ways to give my gravy more flavor, but the one I come back to every time is an ingredient I always have in my pantry.

I’ve been adding a splash of soy sauce to my gravy for years, and it’s one of those little tricks that makes a noticeable difference without anyone being able to put their finger on why.

Soy sauce is rich in umami, the deeply savory flavor that makes foods like mushrooms, Parmesan cheese and the golden crust of a steak so satisfying. Adding a little soy sauce to gravy enhances those same savory flavors, giving it a richness that might otherwise require a longer cooking time. It doesn’t make your gravy taste like soy sauce, provided you use a light hand. It just makes it taste more like really good gravy.

Worcestershire sauce is another popular addition that works for much the same reason, bringing its own combination of savory flavor, acidity and a hint of sweetness. I’ve tried plenty of different additions over the years, and while they all have their merits, soy sauce remains my favorite. I love the depth it brings without competing with the flavors of the turkey and stock.

Sources indicate that the trick with soy sauce is knowing when to add it and, perhaps most importantly, when to stop. You’re not trying to introduce a newly introduced flavor to your gravy so much as coax a little more out of what’s already there. If someone can identify soy sauce in the finished product, you’ve probably been a bit too generous.

Industry observers note that I always add mine at the end, once the gravy has thickened and I’m happy with the consistency. Start with about a teaspoon for every two cups of gravy, stir it in, and give it a taste. Depending on the stock and drippings you’ve used, that may be all you need. If not, add a little more, tasting as you go.

One thing worth remembering is that soy sauce is salty. Very salty, in fact, so save your final seasoning adjustments until after you’ve added it. This is particularly important if you’re using store-bought stock, which may already contain plenty of sodium. Reduced-sodium soy sauce is an option, too, but I generally use the regular stuff and adjust accordingly.

Industry observers note that and don’t save this trick for Thanksgiving! It works beautifully in beef and chicken gravy, too, especially when the pan drippings aren’t quite as flavorful as you’d hoped. A splash of soy sauce won’t make up for a badly made gravy, but it can do an impressive amount of work for an otherwise perfectly respectable one.

Industry observers note that have you used soy sauce in gravy before? Let us know in the comments below!

There are few people I trust more in the kitchen than Nigella Lawson. If she told me to put sardines in a birthday cake, I’d believe her. From the kitchen hacks you’d never expect (like swapping milk for boiling water) to the little techniques that make all the difference in your final bake, this is Nigella Lawson’s best baking advice of all time.

In a recent development, cooking might not require exact measurements, but baking definitely does. “I think every recipe has to be as precise as possible,” Lawson told Vogue in 2018. “Baking, you have to be really precise. If you’re cooking and it suggests 2 to 3 carrots, it doesn’t really matter because they can be different sizes. It’s not going to alter the taste.”.

In a recent development, so, you’ve never really baked before. It’s okay to start small! A three-tier chantilly cake your first day in the kitchen probably isn’t your best bet. “It’s key to go for a simple recipe. Read through the recipe to make sure you understand everything that’s being told to you at the time,” she said. “Look for a recipe that gives you an indication of what to do at each stage. This is what I always say to people: remind yourself you’re not running a restaurant.”.

If you’ve been making your chocolate cake with milk, here’s your sign to stop. Lawson suggests swapping the dairy for hot or boiling water instead to “bloom” the cocoa, dissolve the sugar, and loosen the batter. The result? A crazy moist crumb!

Instead of using plain water when baking bread, Lawson suggests swapping it out for leftover pasta or potato water. “It will help the bread’s texture and rise,” she wrote on X in 2020. “Taste it before adding, though. If very salty, dilute it with fresh water and, obviously, leave any salt in the recipe out.”.

It might sound weird, but Lawson swears by cream of tartar for fluffier, softer scones. “These are the best [ones] I’ve ever eaten, which is quite how it should be since they emanate from one of those old-fashioned cooks who starts a batch the minute the doorbell rings at teatime,” she wrote on her website in 2017. “Yes, I know they look as if they’ve got cellulite—it’s the cream of tartar, which is also why, despite their apparent solidity, they have that dreamy lightness.”.

According to recent reports, lawson’s genius baking hack? DIY self-rising flour. “Nigella tends not to use self-raising flour in her more recent books as she doesn’t bother to keep both plain (all-purpose) and self-raising flour,” her site reads. “Partly because keeping just one type of flour saves on storage space, and partly because if you don’t use self-raising flour regularly, then it will lose its raising power over time.”.

Industry observers note that instead, simply add 2 teaspoons of baking powder for each cup of plain flour. Sift the flour and baking powder together into a bowl before using (and make sure the baking powder is fully integrated), and you’re golden!

We’re all a little extra busy around the holidays, so if you’re planning a dinner party or holiday get-together, it’s okay to make shortcuts. Even Lawson says not everything has to be baked from scratch.

“I have a bit of a weakness for this sort of cake, which is essentially an assembly-job number, a construction of alternate layers of a rich, boozy cream and some store-bought sponge or other,” she told the BBC in 2023 about one of her favorite holiday desserts. “Here the layers comprise a confection of cream and mascarpone, seasonally spiked with Advocaat, full of crystallized ginger, figs and nuts, and that essential component of Christmas: gingerbread.”.

“I am not in the slightest bit insecure about what I can bake, and I’m so very happy doing it, but shop-bought perfection is way beyond me,” she said in a 2014 interview with The Guardian. “But I’m perfectly content with that, and with the ramshackle homemade-ness of my creations.” If that’s good enough for Nigella, it’s good enough for me!

Fall baking has a way of leaving you with awkward amounts of leftover canned pumpkin. So many recipes call for half a can or some other quantity that leaves you wondering what exactly you’re supposed to do with the rest. You put the open can of Libby’s pumpkin puree in the refrigerator with every intention of using it, yet a few days later, there it is, still waiting for you to come up with a plan. It’s not as though you can make half a pumpkin pie.

Fortunately, you don’t need much pumpkin to make something wonderful. In fact, one of the best things I’ve made with leftover pumpkin requires less than a cup, a handful of pantry staples and very little effort. It’s the sort of recipe that makes having leftover pumpkin feel less like a nuisance and more like a stroke of good luck.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

These are a little different from the dense, chewy blondies you might be accustomed to. They have golden edges and a wonderfully soft, almost cakey center, thanks in part to the pumpkin puree. Brown sugar gives them their rich, buttery sweetness, while cinnamon and pumpkin pie spice make them taste unmistakably like fall. The recipe lists the chocolate chips as optional, though I’d argue strongly in favor of including them. Chocolate and pumpkin are excellent together, and the little pockets of melted chocolate are delicious against all those warm spices.

Industry observers note that the pumpkin blondies also almost suspiciously easy to make. Everything comes together in one bowl, using ingredients you probably already have on hand. There’s no frosting to fuss with, no dough to chill and no pie crust to negotiate. Just spread the batter into a 9-inch pan and bake it for 25 to 30 minutes. You’ll have a dozen soft, spiced bars that are equally at home on a Thanksgiving dessert table as they are next to your morning coffee.

It has been revealed that best of all, the recipe calls for just 1/2 cup of canned pumpkin. That’s a particularly convenient amount when you’ve got the remains of another baking project taking up residence in the refrigerator. And if you have a full cup left, making a double batch seems like a perfectly reasonable course of action.

And there’s no reason to limit pumpkin to sweet recipes. A few spoonfuls can add body and richness to soups, pasta dishes and risotto, especially when paired with sage, garlic and Parmesan. Just be sure you’re using plain pumpkin puree rather than pumpkin pie filling, which already contains sugar and spices and isn’t as versatile.

If you’re not quite ready to commit to another pumpkin project, you can always freeze your leftover pumpkin puree. That way, the next time a recipe calls for an odd amount of pumpkin, you’ll have some on hand.

In a recent development, this chocolate mousse cake ticks a lot of boxes—significant, grand, ideal for the holidays, and just enough of a challenge to ensure you feel accomplished. Making the mousse alone will teach you three foundational pastry techniques, and they’re all hidden in plain sight. It starts with a crème anglaise; adding that to chopped chocolate yields a crémeux, and folding in whipped cream turns it into a mousse. Magical. The cake can be easily made from start to finish in the space of a morning, but can be split up further to fit your schedule. Bake the chocolate cake layer and chop all the chocolate on the first day; make the mousse and assemble the cake the following.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

1 hour 30 minutes (plus 6 hours for chilling).

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lay a sheet of parchment paper over base of pan. Fit band on top and clamp shut to hold parchment in place; scrunch up around base. Wrap a sheet of foil around bottom and up sides of pan (this will help prevent any leaking).

Recent findings suggest that whisk together 1 cup (125 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, ⅓ cup (28 g) Dutch-process cocoa powder, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking soda in a medium bowl. Add 1 large egg, ⅓ cup buttermilk, ⅓ cup vegetable oil, 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and ½ cup water and whisk until smooth, about 1 minute. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out with a few moist crumbs attached and top springs back when gently pressed, 25–35 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 10 minutes. Remove band from base; slide cake off parchment and base and onto rack. Let cool completely; discard parchment and foil.

Do Ahead: Cake can be baked 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

In a recent development, place 10.5 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a large heatproof bowl. Bring 1 cup whole milk to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium, about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, vigorously whisk 4 large egg yolks and ½ cup (100 g) sugar in a small heatproof bowl until smooth and lemon yellow, about 1 minute.

Gradually stream hot milk into yolk mixture, whisking constantly until combined. Return to pan, scraping bowl clean with a heatproof rubber spatula. Cook over medium, stirring constantly, until thickened just enough to coat a spoon, about 5 minutes. (Do not let custard come to a boil or it will curdle.) Immediately pour over chocolate; let sit 1 minute. Add 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and whisk vigorously until chocolate is melted and crémeux is smooth.

Beat 1¾ cups heavy cream in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until soft peaks form, about 5 minutes. Add one quarter of whipped cream to crémeux; mix until combined (this will lighten it). Add remaining whipped cream in 3 additions, gently folding after each until incorporated before adding more.

Reassemble springform pan; line bottom with a parchment paper round. Wrap a strip of parchment around inside of pan to create a collar that stands about 1" above band (ends should overlap by at least 3"). Using a large serrated knife, trim off mound on top of cake to create a flat surface if needed. Return cake to pan. Spoon mousse over and smooth into an even layer with an offset spatula or spoon. Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet; chill until top of mousse feels set, about 2 hours.

Place 4 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a medium heatproof bowl. Bring ½ cup heavy cream and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt to a bare simmer in a small saucepan over medium. Pour over chocolate and let sit 2 minutes. Whisk gently until smooth. If ganache feels hot, let cool until lukewarm but still pourable, 8–10 minutes.

Pour ganache over mousse and smooth with offset spatula. Chill until mousse is completely set (ganache will set in about 30 minutes), at least 4 hours and up to 12 hours (no need to cover unless fridge has other strong smells).

According to recent reports, to serve, remove band from base and peel parchment strip away from sides of cake. Transfer cake with base to a plate and let sit 20 minutes; sprinkle top with flaky sea salt.

The nomination of Thumann Severs, who right now serves as senior counsel to Carr, has led to consternation among Democrats due to continued vacancies at the FCC. The five-member commission is intended to have three members of the president’s party, including the chair, and two in the minority.

Right now Carr serves alongside fellow Republican Olivia Trusty and Democrat Anna M. Gomez, whose term expired earlier this year. Gomez may continue to serve through next year under the law if a replacement is not nominated and confirmed.

Democrats are concerned that if Thumann Severs were to be confirmed, the commission’s three Republican members could constitute a quorum on their own, allowing Trump to fire Gomez.

Sources indicate that sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., noted Senate precedent is to move pairs of one Democratic and one Republican nominee for the FCC and that he “strongly” believed the Thumann Severs nomination should have been paired with a renomination of Gomez in order to continue having “both parties at the table.”.

“A bipartisan FCC is essential to avoid things like large-scale media consolidation [and] I think also, more fundamentally, to protect a free and diverse press [that] serves everyone,” Hickenlooper noted.

In addition to urging Trump to renominate Gomez, Democrats underlined the need for a second Democratic member of the commission.

Hickenlooper highlighted Thumann Severs’ close work with Carr, who Democrats and some Republicans have been critical of for comments about using the FCC’s public interest standard against television stations airing programming Carr disagrees with.

Thumann Severs’ work at the FCC currently focuses on the Wireline, Public Safety and Homeland Security, and Consumer and Governmental Affairs bureaus, rather than the Media Bureau.

Committee Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has also been critical of Carr’s comments. On Tuesday, he listed the FCC’s request for ABC-owned stations to submit early license renewals alongside earlier incidents in which he said Democrats encouraged the weaponization of the FCC against conservative voices.

Recent findings suggest that “The First Amendment places key limits on the government’s ability to regulate speech,” Cruz said. “The FCC possesses significant regulatory authority over communications, so there is always a risk that it could weaponize its authority against Americans with whom it disagrees.”.

Thumann Severs committed to Cruz that she would base licensing decisions on “the law and the record” and not use the FCC’s authority to “pressure or punish” broadcasters for protected speech.

However, when Sen. Edward J. Markey, D-Mass., questioned Thumann Severs on whether the FCC could punish broadcasters the president disagreed with, Thumann Severs repeated one of Carr’s arguments in discussing the FCC’s role.

It has been revealed that “Broadcasters are subject to public interest obligations as part of the public trustee model in exchange for the licenses that they hold,” she mentioned. “As part of those public interest obligations, they are subject to many different rules and requirements, and the FCC is charged with enforcing and investigating the public interest standard against broadcasters.”.

Under repeated questions from Markey about Carr’s previous remarks, Thumann Severs noted she would base her decisions “in the facts and the law and the record.”.

Sources indicate that luján also asked Thumann Severs to name concerns where she had disagreed with Carr or Trump. While she noted her decisions would be her own, she declined to name any examples of disagreement.

In addition to questions about Carr, Democrats asked the nominee about the FCC’s E-Rate program, which provides low-cost connectivity for schools and libraries, and the Universal Service Fund, which funds the E-Rate program and other programs.

According to recent reports, thumann Severs mentioned that she believes the E-Rate program has been successful and that the FCC has a statutory obligation to provide some kind of discounted service to schools and libraries. But she was less forthcoming on whether the FCC could shut down the program as it right now exists without congressional approval or whether the program should be restricted only to rural areas.

Late last month, Democratic members of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, led by Communications and Technology Subcommittee ranking member Doris Matsui, D-Calif., sent a letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Cruz urging Gomez’s renomination with any move to confirm a Republican nominee.

Sources indicate that “Commissioner Gomez has shown the experience and judgment to continue that work,” the members wrote. “We therefore ask that the Senate pair any fresh Republican nominee with her renomination to a full term, consistent with the bipartisan design Congress built into this agency.”.

On Monday, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights also sent a letter to committee leadership urging a delay on the hearing and any vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination until Gomez can be renominated.

“Independent agencies should not be extensions of presidential will: their leaders should exercise independent judgement based on their expertise and statutory mandates,” the group wrote.

Cruz did not indicate Tuesday when the committee might vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination, and no markup has yet been announced by the committee of hers' and those of three others for two posts at NASA and one at the Transportation Department who also testified.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recipe by LaDonna Reed, Ponca City, Oklahoma.

Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

It takes just 25 minutes to make chicken broccoli Alfredo by combining veggies and meat in a creamy garlic and Parmesan sauce.

In a recent development, I love dishes that make it feel like you’re treating the family to a dinner at a restaurant, and anything with Alfredo definitely falls into that category. And yet, even though the cream sauce in this chicken broccoli Alfredo is made from scratch, it’s actually totally doable at home. (Plus there’s no need to dress up to go out to eat—you can enjoy this meal in your pajamas if you want to!).

It has been revealed that there are a lot of ways to adapt this chicken Alfredo recipe using up other ingredients you might have on hand. Make it with chicken breasts as written, or swap in chicken thighs or leftover rotisserie chicken instead. Use fresh broccoli or pull those frozen florets from the freezer. Spice up the Parmesan sauce with a little extra cayenne pepper, or add a swirl of herby pesto.

Industry observers note that cook the fettuccine according to the package directions for al dente. Add the broccoli florets to the water for the last five minutes of cooking.

Editor’s Tip: Here’s what al dente actually means, and how to achieve it in your fettuccine and other pastas.

Meanwhile, in a large skillet, cook the chicken and chopped onion in butter until the chicken is no longer pink. Add the minced garlic, salt and cayenne pepper, and cook for one minute longer. Stir in the flour until it’s blended with the other ingredients.

Recent findings suggest that gradually add the half-and-half, thawed peas and Parmesan cheese to the skillet. Bring the mixture to a boil. Cook and stir the sauce for one to two minutes or until it’s thickened.

It has been revealed that drain the fettuccine and broccoli, and toss them with the chicken mixture. Serve the chicken broccoli Alfredo while it’s hot.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

According to recent reports, once the chicken broccoli Alfredo cools, transfer it to a sealed food storage container. Store it in the refrigerator for up to four days.

It has been revealed that yes, you can prepare this dish up to three days ahead of time. Gently reheat the chicken broccoli Alfredo in a covered skillet on the stove.

Sources indicate that the creamy sauce in this Alfredo recipe may separate and turn watery when frozen and then thawed. To protect the texture, it’s best not to freeze chicken broccoli Alfredo.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

It has been revealed that yes, you can substitute cubed chicken thighs for the chicken breast. Cook the thighs in butter until the internal temperature reaches 170°F.

Save a little time by using meat from a cooked rotisserie chicken. Cube or shred the breast meat—or a combination of breast and dark meat. Add the chicken to the sauce near the end of cooking time to warm it through.

Industry observers note that yes, frozen broccoli can be substituted for fresh. Add the frozen florets to the pasta water a couple of minutes before the end of cooking time to blanch them.

Below is a tight curation of the best early black Friday deals, so far.

Recent findings suggest that believe it or not, there’s another shopping platform to peruse—say hello to Shop, the consumer-facing sister of Shopify. Everything from those buzzy direct-to-consumer brands to K-beauty favorites is in one place, with no tab-hopping. What to buy? The “everything store” seems to have deals on everything—and sometimes that means sorting through bizarre, random products to find what you’re actually looking for. Plus, tried-and-true makeup brushes from Sigma, for those looking to szoosh up the makeup tools.

Beauty is Bluemercury’s specialty—offering everything from wellness essentials and makeup deals to premium moisturizers, viral mascaras, and even the brand’s coveted annual Advent calendar. While the deals are just starting to roll in, there’s plenty more to come. Right now, the Holiday Shopping Party is in full swing. Cross $200 and the whole order drops 20%, cross $800 and the savings climbs to 25%, and if you’re a significant spender, cross $1,500 and you’ll get 30% off.

One of the main beauty mega-retailers stateside is Ulta Beauty—a wonderland of beauty, everything from affordable to prestige prices in just about every sub-category.

#31631. Best Cutting Boards for Slicing, Dicing, and Chopping (2026)
